public_rationale: Marcus's general lesson is that polished LLM output often contains subtle errors that people miss, as in early ChatGPT days. Independent studies back the core of this. A 2023 peer-reviewed study found 52% of ChatGPT programming answers had incorrect information. Its users, helped by the answers' well-written style, missed the misinformation 39% of the time. In February 2025, BBC journalists judged 51% of answers from four major assistants to have significant issues. The Tow Center found AI search tools' confident tone made errors hard to tell apart from correct answers. The 'most people' part is not measured directly: the one figure found (39% missed) is below a majority, though it comes from programmers who could check with tools.
limitations: 'Most people wouldn't catch' is not directly quantified. The one user study shows a substantial minority of misses, among programmers who could check with tools.
The studies cover particular tasks (programming, news), not all LLM use.
The supported rating depends on a plain reading of 'often'.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: As in the early ChatGPT days, LLM output often contains subtle errors most people would not catch, however good it looks, so users should beware.
conditions: no matter how good-looking the output

statement.excerpt: The primary lesson here is the same as in the early ChatGPT days: caveat emptor. No matter how good-looking the output, there are often subtle errors that most people wouldn’t catch.

from_speaker: the same as in the early ChatGPT days
No matter how good-looking the output
our_interpretation: Reading: from ChatGPT's launch through early 2025, polished output from general LLM chatbots often (a meaningful share of answers, not rare) contained factual errors. Ordinary users would often fail to notice those errors because the answers look fluent and confident.
Target period runs from ChatGPT's launch (2022-11) to the post date, since he says the lesson is the same then and now.
'Most people wouldn't catch' is not quantified anywhere. Evidence that fluent, confident answers lead users to miss a substantial share of errors counts in favour.
criteria.support_condition: Independent studies from 2022-11 to 2025-02 show a substantial share of polished LLM answers contain factual errors, and that users frequently fail to detect them.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Independent studies from that period show LLM answers rarely contained errors, or that users reliably caught the errors that did occur.

evidence.excerpt: 51% of all AI responses were flagged as having ‘significant issues’ of some form by reviewers.
evidence.explanation: Expert journalists found about half of ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini and Perplexity answers about the news had significant issues. That shows errors in polished assistant output were common, not rare.

evidence.excerpt: 52% of ChatGPT answers contain incorrect information and 77% are verbose. Nonetheless, our user study participants still preferred ChatGPT answers 35% of the time due to their comprehensiveness and well-articulated language style. However, they also overlooked the misinformation in the ChatGPT answers 39% of the time.
evidence.explanation: In the early-ChatGPT era, about half of answers had errors. Even programmers who were allowed to check with external tools missed the misinformation 39% of the time, partly because the answers were well written. That fits 'good-looking output' hiding errors.

evidence.excerpt: their authoritative conversational tone, which can make it difficult for users to distinguish between accurate and inaccurate information.
evidence.locator: section 'Premium models provided more confidently incorrect answers than their free counterparts', paragraph 2

evidence.explanation: Independent testers in February 2025 found AI search tools were often wrong, and judged that their confident tone makes errors hard for users to spot.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: A representative study of ordinary users' ability to detect subtle errors in fluent LLM answers would settle the 'most people' part.
